author: NASA, ESA, and A. Simon (Goddard Space Flight Center)
caption: Jupiter has far more mass than the Earth, so its gravity is much stronger: the same object would weigh about two and a half times as much there.

author: Gregory H. Revera
caption: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so its gravity is only about one sixth as strong: an astronaut's weight is smaller there, but her mass is the same.

author: NASA JSC ISS image library
caption: A steel container ship about 400 m long in Egypt's Suez Canal, photographed from the International Space Station: its wide, hollow hull pushes aside enough water to float.

author: Niels Johannes
caption: Load-line marks on a ship's side: the more cargo it carries, the lower it sits, and the water must never rise above the correct line, or the ship could sink.

author: Pseudopanax at English Wikipedia
caption: Still water is very smooth, so it reflects light regularly, like a plane mirror, and we see a clear upside-down image of the mountains and trees.

author: ajizai
caption: A real ray of light through a glass block: it bends towards the normal as it enters the glass, away from the normal as it leaves, and comes out parallel to the ray that went in.

author: Meganbeckett27
caption: The pencil looks bent at the water surface because light from the part under water is refracted as it passes from the water into the air.

author: Glenn Ashton
caption: Pink granite from Aswan close up: large pink, white and dark crystals fit tightly together in random directions — the sign of an igneous rock that cooled slowly.

author: Vassil
caption: A nummulite fossil split open to show the coiled chambers of its shell; fossils like this can be seen in many of the limestone blocks of the Giza pyramids.

author: Siim
caption: Gneiss, a metamorphic rock: heat and pressure lined its crystals up into light and dark bands.

author: Further to Fly
caption: The fossil skeleton of Dorudon, an ancient whale, in the desert at Wadi El-Hitan, Fayoum: proof that this dry land was once covered by the sea.

author: Jan Nyssen
caption: Basalt, an igneous rock made when lava cooled quickly at the surface: its crystals are too small to see without a hand lens.

author: Vyacheslav Argenberg
caption: The White Desert near Farafra, Egypt: wind and blown sand have weathered and eroded the soft white chalk into towers, leaving sand and rock pieces around them.

author: Mx. Granger
caption: Layers of sedimentary rock in the Grand Canyon, USA: each band was once sediment laid down flat, and the lowest layers are the oldest.

author: Wilfredor
caption: Soil with a lot of clay shrinks and cracks into hard plates when it dries out; when it is wet it becomes sticky and drains slowly.

author: Jacques Descloitres, MODIS Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC
caption: Egypt from space: the green farmland of the Nile Valley and Delta grows on dark silt left by the river, while the land on either side is sandy desert.

author: NASA, ESA, and A. Simon (Goddard Space Flight Center)
caption: Jupiter, the largest planet, photographed by the Hubble Space Telescope: we see the tops of its clouds, and the orange oval is a giant storm called the Great Red Spot.

author: NASA / JPL / Space Science Institute
caption: Saturn photographed by the Cassini spacecraft: a giant planet made mostly of gas, with the brightest and easiest-to-see rings in the Solar System.

author: Gregory H. Revera
caption: A full Moon: the whole half that faces us is lit by the Sun. The Moon gives out no light of its own; we see sunlight reflected from its rocky surface.

author: Wxao Zexw
caption: A thin waxing crescent seen a few days after new moon: only a small part of the Moon's sunlit half faces us.

author: jburgin (Flickr)
caption: A bicycle brake: when the rider brakes, the rubber block presses on the wheel rim, and friction between the two surfaces acts against the motion and slows the bicycle.

author: Tony Hisgett from Birmingham, UK
caption: A dolphin's smooth, pointed, streamlined shape gives it less water resistance, so it can move quickly through the water.

author: KMJ
caption: Inside a filament lamp: current flows through the very thin coiled wire (the filament), which gets hot and glows. If the filament breaks, the lamp has 'blown' and leaves a gap in the circuit.
